claim: Intramuscular implantation of Kras (G12V)-expressing, Cdkn2a (p16p19) deficient mouse myofiber-associated (MFA) cells into the extremity muscles of NOD.SCID mice induces rapid sarcoma formation.
source: We previously reported rapid sarcoma induction by intramuscular implantation of Kras (G12V)-expressing, Cdkn2a (p16p19) deficient mouse myofiber-associated (MFA) cells into the extremity muscles of NOD. SCID mice (Hettmer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hettmer et al., 2011) and is part of the experimental system described in the manuscript.

claim: Transcriptional profiling of Kras;p16p19null sarcomas identified a cluster of sarcoma-relevant candidate genes enriched in mouse sarcomas and human RMS compared to normal skeletal muscle.
source: Transcriptional profiling of Kras; p16p19null sarcomas identified a cluster of sarcoma-relevant candidate genes. These genes are enriched in mouse sarcomas and in human RMS as compared to normal mouse or human skeletal muscle (Hettmer et al., 2011), and may include transcripts of fundamental importance for sarcoma growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hettmer et al., 2011) describing transcriptional profiling results.

claim: Silencing of asparagine synthetase (ASNS) produced the strongest inhibitory effect on sarcoma growth in a functional genomic screen of mouse sarcomas.
source: In both RMS and NMS cells, silencing of ASNS (Asparagine Synthetase) produced by far the strongest anti-proliferative effect (p<0.0001, q<0.01, 4–5 of 5 shRNAs with FDR<30%; Figure 1D,I and Supplementary files 5–6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the shRNA screen with statistical significance (p<0.0001, q<0.01) and reference to Figure 1D,I showing the results.

claim: ASNS silencing in mouse Kras;p16p19null RMS cells reduced growth to 30.16% of control cells.
source: ASNS silencing reduced the growth of Kras;p16p19null RMS and NMS cells to 30.16% and 6.69% of the average of control RMS and NMS cells, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from the proliferation screen.

claim: ASNS silencing in mouse Kras;p16p19null NMS cells reduced growth to 6.69% of control cells.
source: ASNS silencing reduced the growth of Kras;p16p19null RMS and NMS cells to 30.16% and 6.69% of the average of control RMS and NMS cells, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from the proliferation screen.

claim: Effective depletion of ASNS protein by target-specific shRNAs was confirmed by Western Blot.
source: Effective depletion of ASNS protein by the target-specific shRNAs employed in our screen was confirmed by Western Blot (Figure 1E,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 1E,J.

claim: Asparagine supplementation at 100 mg/L reversed the growth inhibition observed in shASNS-infected Kras;p16p19null RMS cells.
source: Supplementation of the culture media with 100 mg/L asparagine reversed the growth inhibition observed in shASNS-infected Kras;p16p19null RMS (Figure 2A-2B) and NMS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-1B) cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-2B demonstrating rescue of growth inhibition.

claim: Asparagine supplementation at 100 mg/L reversed the growth inhibition observed in shASNS-infected Kras;p16p19null NMS cells.
source: Supplementation of the culture media with 100 mg/L asparagine reversed the growth inhibition observed in shASNS-infected Kras;p16p19null RMS (Figure 2A-2B) and NMS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-1B) cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-1B demonstrating rescue of growth inhibition.

claim: Asparagine supplementation at 10 mg/L reversed the growth inhibition of shASNS-transduced Kras;p16p19null RMS and NMS cells.
source: Dose response analysis revealed that reversal of growth inhibiton of shASNS-transduced Kras;p16p19null RMS and NMS cells was also observed at 10 mg/L asparagine, whereas 0.01, 0.1 or 1 mg/L asparagine were insufficient (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Asparagine concentrations of 0.01, 0.1, or 1 mg/L were insufficient to reverse growth inhibition of shASNS-transduced Kras;p16p19null RMS and NMS cells.
source: Dose response analysis revealed that reversal of growth inhibiton of shASNS-transduced Kras;p16p19null RMS and NMS cells was also observed at 10 mg/L asparagine, whereas 0.01, 0.1 or 1 mg/L asparagine were insufficient (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Asparagine supplementation did not reverse the growth inhibitory effect of shRNA-mediated silencing of Kras in Kras;p16p19null RMS cells.
source: Asparagine supplementation did not reverse the growth inhibitory effect of shRNA-mediated silencing of Kras in Kras;p16p19null RMS cells (Figure 2A-2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-2B demonstrating specificity of asparagine rescue.

claim: The growth-inhibitory effects of ASNS silencing on mouse sarcoma cells result from cellular asparagine starvation.
source: Taken together, we conclude that the growth-inhibitory effects of ASNS silencing on mouse sarcoma cells result from cellular asparagine starvation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that exogenous asparagine reverses ASNS silencing effects.

claim: Asns silencing in mouse Kras;p16p19null RMS cells caused an increase in the fraction of sarcoma cells undergoing apoptosis (p<0.001).
source: Asns silencing in mouse Kras;p16p19null RMS cells caused an increase in the fraction of sarcoma cells undergoing apoptosis, as determined by staining with propidium iodide (PI) and Annexin V (p<0.001, Figure 2C-2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PI/Annexin V staining shown in Figure 2C-2D with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Asns silencing reduced the percentage of BrdU+ cells in S phase in mouse Kras;p16p19null RMS cells (p<0.001).
source: Moreover, Asns silencing reduced the percentage of BrdU + cells in S phase (p<0.001, Figure 2E-2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BrdU staining shown in Figure 2E-2F with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Both the increase in apoptosis and reduction in S phase cells caused by Asns silencing were reversed by exogenous asparagine supplementation.
source: Both effects were reversed by exogenous asparagine supplementation (Figure 2D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,F demonstrating rescue of both phenotypes.

claim: shASNS-infected Kras;p16p19null RMS cells exhibited minimal OP-puromycin staining, indicating reduced polypeptide synthesis.
source: Similarly, shASNS-infected cells exhibited only minimal OP-puromycin staining (Figure 2G, upper left panel), while synthesis of new polypeptides was restored in shASNS-infected sarcoma cells grown in medium supplemented with asparagine (Figure 2G, lower left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by OP-puromycin staining data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Synthesis of new polypeptides was restored in shASNS-infected sarcoma cells grown in medium supplemented with asparagine.
source: Similarly, shASNS-infected cells exhibited only minimal OP-puromycin staining (Figure 2G, upper left panel), while synthesis of new polypeptides was restored in shASNS-infected sarcoma cells grown in medium supplemented with asparagine (Figure 2G, lower left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by OP-puromycin staining data shown in Figure 2G demonstrating rescue of protein synthesis.

claim: Rapidly proliferating shLUC-infected Kras;p16p19null RMS cells exhibited strong OP-puromycin staining, indicating brisk polypeptide synthesis.
source: Rapidly proliferating shLUC-infected Kras;p16p19null RMS cells exhibited strong OP-puromycin staining, indicating brisk polypeptide synthesis (Figure 2G, middle panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by OP-puromycin staining data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Blockade of protein translation by exposure to cycloheximide abrogated OP-puromycin staining.
source: However, blockade of protein translation by exposure to cycloheximide abrogated OP-puromycin staining (Figure 2G, far right panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G validating the OP-puromycin method.

claim: Similar effects of ASNS silencing on apoptosis, cell cycle and synthesis of nascent peptide chains were observed in Kras;p16p19null NMS cells.
source: Similar effects of ASNS silencing on apoptosis, cell cycle and synthesis of nascent peptide chains were observed in Kras;p16p19null NMS cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ASNS was detected in 16 of 22 (73%) human RMS cores by immunohistochemistry.
source: ASNS was detected in 16 of 22 (73%) human RMS cores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and in 12 of 27 (44%) human leiomyosarcoma cores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from tissue arrays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ASNS was detected in 12 of 27 (44%) human leiomyosarcoma cores by immunohistochemistry.
source: ASNS was detected in 16 of 22 (73%) human RMS cores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and in 12 of 27 (44%) human leiomyosarcoma cores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from tissue arrays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Increased expression of ASNS compared to normal human muscle was detected in 9 of 9 human sarcoma cell lines analyzed by PCR.
source: Also, increased expression of ASNS compared to normal human muscle was detected in 9 of 9 human sarcoma cell lines analyzed by PCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), including the PAX3:FOXO1-positive human RMS cell line Rh30.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of ASNS in Rh30 cells reduced proliferation (p<0.001).
source: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of ASNS in Rh30 cells (Figure 3A) reduced proliferation (p<0.001; Figure 3B–C), increased the percentage of apoptotic cells (p<0.01; Figure 3D–E), reduced the percentage of cells in S phase (p<0.001; Figure 3F–G) and impeded nascent polypeptide synthesis (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of ASNS in Rh30 cells increased the percentage of apoptotic cells (p<0.01).
source: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of ASNS in Rh30 cells (Figure 3A) reduced proliferation (p<0.001; Figure 3B–C), increased the percentage of apoptotic cells (p<0.01; Figure 3D–E), reduced the percentage of cells in S phase (p<0.001; Figure 3F–G) and impeded nascent polypeptide synthesis (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-E with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of ASNS in Rh30 cells reduced the percentage of cells in S phase (p<0.001).
source: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of ASNS in Rh30 cells (Figure 3A) reduced proliferation (p<0.001; Figure 3B–C), increased the percentage of apoptotic cells (p<0.01; Figure 3D–E), reduced the percentage of cells in S phase (p<0.001; Figure 3F–G) and impeded nascent polypeptide synthesis (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F-G with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of ASNS in Rh30 cells impeded nascent polypeptide synthesis.
source: ShRNA-mediated knockdown of ASNS in Rh30 cells (Figure 3A) reduced proliferation (p<0.001; Figure 3B–C), increased the percentage of apoptotic cells (p<0.01; Figure 3D–E), reduced the percentage of cells in S phase (p<0.001; Figure 3F–G) and impeded nascent polypeptide synthesis (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by OP-puromycin staining data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The effects of ASNS silencing on Rh30 growth and peptide synthesis were reversed by asparagine supplementation.
source: The effects of ASNS silencing on Rh30 growth and peptide synthesis were reversed by asparagine supplementation (Figure 3B–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-H demonstrating rescue effects.

claim: ASNS silencing in human Rh30 cells recapitulated the inhibitory effects on cell growth and polypeptide synthesis observed in mouse Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells.
source: Thus, ASNS silencing in human Rh30 cells recapitulated the inhibitory effects on cell growth and polypeptide synthesis observed in mouse Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparing the experimental results from human Rh30 cells to mouse sarcoma cells.

claim: Both amino sulfoximine 5 (AS5) and asparaginase reduced the proliferation of mouse and human sarcoma cell lines in vitro.
source: Both amino sulfoximine 5 (AS5) and asparaginase reduced the proliferation of mouse and human sarcoma cell lines in vitro (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: For asparaginase, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 0.2–0.5 IU/ml in mouse Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells.
source: For asparaginase, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 0.2–0.5 IU/ml in mouse Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells, 0.8–0.9 IU/ml in human HT1080, Rh30 and Rh41 cells and 6 IU/ml in human RD cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: For asparaginase, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 0.8–0.9 IU/ml in human HT1080, Rh30 and Rh41 cells.
source: For asparaginase, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 0.2–0.5 IU/ml in mouse Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells, 0.8–0.9 IU/ml in human HT1080, Rh30 and Rh41 cells and 6 IU/ml in human RD cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: For asparaginase, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 6 IU/ml in human RD cells.
source: For asparaginase, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 0.2–0.5 IU/ml in mouse Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells, 0.8–0.9 IU/ml in human HT1080, Rh30 and Rh41 cells and 6 IU/ml in human RD cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: For the ASNS inhibitor AS5, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 80–150 μM in mouse Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells.
source: For the ASNS inhibitor AS5, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 80–150 μM in mouse Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells and 200–300 μM in the human sarcoma cell lines tested (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: For the ASNS inhibitor AS5, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 200–300 μM in the human sarcoma cell lines tested.
source: For the ASNS inhibitor AS5, EC50 concentrations were estimated at 80–150 μM in mouse Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells and 200–300 μM in the human sarcoma cell lines tested (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: The growth-inhibitory effects of chemical ASNS inhibition by AS5 were reversed by exogenous asparagine supplementation.
source: Similar to previous observations in cells that underwent genetic inhibition of ASNS, the growth-inhibitory effects of chemical ASNS inhibition by AS5 were reversed by exogenous asparagine supplementation (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D demonstrating rescue of AS5 effects.

claim: The growth inhibitory effects of AS5 result from asparagine deprivation of sarcoma cells.
source: These findings strongly suggest that the growth inhibitory effects of AS5 result from asparagine deprivation of sarcoma cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that exogenous asparagine reverses AS5 effects.

claim: Tumors arising from shASNS RMS cells expressed less ASNS than tumors arising from shLUC cells.
source: IHC showed that tumors arising from shASNS cells expressed less ASNS than tumors arising from shLUC cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was no difference in latency of shASNS- and shLUC-tumors (p = 0.3).
source: However, there was no difference in latency of shASNS- and shLUC-tumors (p = 0.3; Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor latency data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis (p = 0.3).

claim: Normal asparagine concentrations in mouse and human plasma were previously reported to be between 3.8 mg/L and 7.3 mg/L.
source: As normal asparagine concentrations in mouse and human plasma were previously reported to be between 3.8 mg/L and 7.3 mg/L (Cooney et al., 1970), these data suggest that freely available asparagine in mouse serum and tissue might counteract the effects of tumor-specific ASNS silencing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Cooney et al., 1970) reporting plasma asparagine concentrations.

claim: Freely available asparagine in mouse serum and tissue might counteract the effects of tumor-specific ASNS silencing.
source: As normal asparagine concentrations in mouse and human plasma were previously reported to be between 3.8 mg/L and 7.3 mg/L (Cooney et al., 1970), these data suggest that freely available asparagine in mouse serum and tissue might counteract the effects of tumor-specific ASNS silencing.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on known plasma asparagine levels and in vitro rescue data.

claim: Asparaginase treatment at 1500 IU/kg by daily intraperitoneal injection was well tolerated by the animals without significant weight loss.
source: This dosage was well tolerated by the animals without significant weight loss (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by weight monitoring data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Serum asparagine levels were reduced 13-fold in asparaginase-treated mice (0.53 mg/L (4 μM) versus 6.87 mg/L (52 μM) in untreated mice, p<0.001).
source: Serum asparagine levels were reduced 13-fold in asparaginase-treated mice (0.53 mg/L (4 μM) versus 6.87 mg/L (52 μM) in untreated mice, p<0.001; Figure 5D and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 5D and Supplementary file 7 with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Daily exposure to asparaginase did not change the latency of shLUC-tumors (p = 0.5).
source: Daily exposure to asparaginase did not change the latency of shLUC-tumors (p = 0.5; Figure 5B); however, asparaginase treatment significantly prolonged tumor latency in mice implanted with shASNS-RMS cells (p<0.001; Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor latency data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis (p = 0.5).

claim: Asparaginase treatment significantly prolonged tumor latency in mice implanted with shASNS-RMS cells (p<0.001).
source: Daily exposure to asparaginase did not change the latency of shLUC-tumors (p = 0.5; Figure 5B); however, asparaginase treatment significantly prolonged tumor latency in mice implanted with shASNS-RMS cells (p<0.001; Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor latency data shown in Figure 5B with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: 2 out of 8 mice implanted with shASNS-RMS cells and treated with asparaginase did not develop tumors during 4 months of follow up after tumor cell injection.
source: Moreover, 2 out of 8 mice in this experimental group did not develop tumors during 4 months of follow up after tumor cell injection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation data from the in vivo transplantation study.

claim: Similar effects were observed when NOD.SCID mice were transplanted with shASNS-infected and shLUC-infected Kras;p16p19null NMS cells.
source: Similar effects were observed when NOD. SCID mice were transplanted with shASNS-infected and shLUC-infected Kras; p16p19null NMS cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ASNS inhibition combined with depletion of plasma asparagine reduces sarcoma growth in vivo.
source: Thus, ASNS inhibition combined with depletion of plasma asparagine reduces sarcoma growth in vivo.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the in vivo transplantation experiments showing delayed tumor latency with combined ASNS silencing and asparaginase treatment.

claim: ASNS is the amidotransferase that converts L-aspartic acid into L-asparagine in an energy-consuming enzymatic reaction requiring ATP and a nitrogen source that is L-glutamine in eukaryotic cells.
source: ASNS is the amidotransferase that converts L-aspartic acid into L-asparagine in an energy-consuming enzymatic reaction requiring ATP and a nitrogen source that is L-glutamine in eukaryotic cells (Richards and Kilberg, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Richards and Kilberg, 2006) describing ASNS biochemistry.

claim: Depletion of functional ASNS in both mouse and human RMS cells reduced the proportion of cells in S phase and impeded synthesis of nascent polypeptide chains.
source: Depletion of functional ASNS in both mouse and human RMS cells reduced the proportion of cells in S phase and impeded synthesis of nascent polypetide chains.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from the BrdU and OP-puromycin assays.

claim: ASNS silencing in melanoma cells was recently reported to result in cell cycle arrest.
source: Similarly, ASNS silencing in melanoma cells was recently reported to result in cell cycle arrest (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Li et al., 2015) on melanoma cells.

claim: Rapidly growing sarcoma cells depend on adequate availability of intrinsic or extrinsic asparagine to support tumor growth.
source: The effects of ASNS reduction in sarcoma cells were reversed by exogenous supplementation with asparagine, supporting the notion that rapidly growing sarcoma cells depend on adequate availability of intrinsic or extrinsic asparagine to support tumor growth.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that exogenous asparagine reverses ASNS silencing effects.

claim: ASNS inhibition significantly slowed mouse sarcoma growth in vivo only when combined with depletion of plasma asparagine.
source: Moreover, ASNS inhibition significantly slowed mouse sarcoma growth in vivo only when combined with depletion of plasma asparagine, likely reflecting the ability of systemic asparagine in the tumor environment to replenish intracellular asparagine availability after ASNS inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by the in vivo transplantation experiments showing that ASNS silencing alone did not delay tumor latency, but combined with asparaginase treatment it did.

claim: Systemic asparagine in the tumor environment can replenish intracellular asparagine availability after ASNS inhibition.
source: Moreover, ASNS inhibition significantly slowed mouse sarcoma growth in vivo only when combined with depletion of plasma asparagine, likely reflecting the ability of systemic asparagine in the tumor environment to replenish intracellular asparagine availability after ASNS inhibition.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that ASNS silencing alone did not delay tumor growth in vivo.

claim: Asparagine reliance of sarcoma cells represents a metabolic vulnerability that could be exploited therapeutically to inhibit rapid tumor growth.
source: We speculate that asparagine reliance of sarcoma cells represents a metabolic vulnerability that could be exploited therapeutically to inhibit rapid tumor growth.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings showing asparagine dependence.

claim: Asparagine and glycine are metabolites that are heavily consumed by cancer cell lines.
source: Previously published metabolic profiling studies have identified a number of metabolites that are heavily consumed by cancer cell lines, including glycine and asparagine (Jain et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Jain et al., 2012) on metabolic profiling.

claim: Glycine starvation prolonged the G1 phase of the cell cycle and reduced proliferation, in part because sufficient amounts of this amino acid are required to support de novo purine biosynthesis in rapidly dividing cells.
source: Glycine starvation prolonged the G1 phase of the cell cycle and reduced proliferation, in part because sufficient amounts of this amino acid are required to support de novo purine biosynthesis in rapidly dividing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Jain et al., 2012) on glycine starvation effects.

claim: Protein synthesis in glycine-starved cells remained relatively intact.
source: Unlike purine synthesis, protein synthesis in glycine-starved cells remained relatively intact (Jain et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Jain et al., 2012) on glycine starvation effects.

claim: Asparagine starvation of mouse and human sarcoma cells impedes synthesis of nascent polypeptide chains thereby slowing cell proliferation.
source: In contrast, we found that asparagine starvation of mouse and human sarcoma cells impedes synthesis of nascent polypeptide chains thereby slowing cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the OP-puromycin and proliferation assay data from the manuscript.

claim: Free asparagine levels in developing seeds correlate positively with higher protein levels at maturity in soybean, barley and maize.
source: These results are consistent with observations in soybean, barley and maize where free asparagine levels in developing seeds correlate positively with higher protein levels at maturity (Pandurangan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Pandurangan et al., 2012) on plant biology.

claim: Limiting the extracellular supply or blocking the synthesis of single amino acids is known to suppress global translation initiation via activation of GCN2 and phosphorylation of the translation initiation factor EIF2α.
source: Moreover, limiting the extracellular supply or blocking the synthesis of single amino acids is known to suppress global translation initiation via activation of GCN2 and phosphorylation of the translation initiation factor EIF2α (Sood et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sood et al., 2000) on amino acid starvation and translation control.

claim: Asparagine in the tumor cell environment may have important functions in controlling the synthesis and turnover of protein in sarcoma cells.
source: Thus, asparagine in the tumor cell environment may have important functions in controlling the synthesis and turnover of protein in sarcoma cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings and cited literature on amino acid control of translation.

claim: Aspartate carries reducing equivalents in the malate-aspartate shuttle.
source: For instance, our data do not exclude the possibility that glutamate deprivation and/or aspartate excess resulting from changes in asparagine biosynthesis negatively impact cell survival and proliferation. However, aspartate carries reducing equivalents in the malate-aspartate shuttle (Son et al., 2013), and increased aspartate levels after ASNS knockdown might be predicted to benefit the redox state of sarcoma cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Son et al., 2013) on the malate-aspartate shuttle.

claim: Increased aspartate levels after ASNS knockdown might be predicted to benefit the redox state of sarcoma cells.
source: However, aspartate carries reducing equivalents in the malate-aspartate shuttle (Son et al., 2013), and increased aspartate levels after ASNS knockdown might be predicted to benefit the redox state of sarcoma cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on known biochemistry of the malate-aspartate shuttle.

claim: Increased glutaminase expression in cancer cells can counterbalance decreased glutamate levels, especially in a glutamine-rich environment.
source: In addition, it has been suggested that increased glutaminase expression in cancer cells can counterbalance decreased glutamate levels, especially in a glutamine-rich environment (Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Huang et al., 2014) on glutaminase expression.

claim: Glutaminase expression was increased by 7- to 11-fold in mouse sarcoma cells compared to normal mouse muscle.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that glutaminase expression was increased by 7- to 11-fold in mouse sarcoma cells compared to normal mouse muscle (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that this mechanism may be used by sarcoma cells to counteract glutamate reductions that may result from ASNS silencing.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Increased glutaminase expression may be used by sarcoma cells to counteract glutamate reductions that may result from ASNS silencing.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that glutaminase expression was increased by 7- to 11-fold in mouse sarcoma cells compared to normal mouse muscle (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that this mechanism may be used by sarcoma cells to counteract glutamate reductions that may result from ASNS silencing.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed glutaminase expression and cited literature.

claim: Asparagine supplementation can suppress cell death in glutamine-deprived cells.
source: Finally, a recent report demonstrated, unexpectedly, that asparagine supplementation can suppress cell death in glutamine-deprived cells (Zhang et al., 2014), implicating asparagine in promoting cellular adaptation to metabolic stresses such as glutamine depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Zhang et al., 2014) on asparagine and glutamine deprivation.

claim: Asparagine is the last amino acid synthesized in the TCA cycle and its amination depends exclusively on glutamine.
source: This study also noted that asparagine is the last amino acid synthesized in the TCA cycle and that its amination depends exclusively on glutamine (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Zhang et al., 2014) on asparagine biosynthesis.

claim: Amino acid availability is known to stimulate mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1, which integrates environmental and intracellular signals to regulate cell growth.
source: Amino acid availability is known to stimulate mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1, which integrates environmental and intracellular signals to regulate cell growth (Jewell et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Jewell et al., 2015) on mTOR signaling.

claim: Asparagine may serve a central role as a cellular sensor of TCA cycle intermediate/reduced nitrogen availability and as a metabolic regulator of cell behavior.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that asparagine may serve a central role as a cellular sensor of TCA cycle intermediate/ reduced nitrogen availability and, ultimately, as a metabolic regulator of cell behavior.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on cited literature about asparagine's role in metabolism and signaling.

claim: The shRNA proliferation screen did not comprehensively evaluate all amino acid biosynthetic pathways.
source: The shRNA proliferation screen we performed was designed to evaluate the functional contributions of a particular group of sarcoma signature genes identified by their high level expression in both Ras-driven mouse sarcomas and human sarcomas, and thus did not comprehensively evaluate all amino acid biosynthetic pathways.
evidence: The claim is an explicit statement about the design limitations of the screen.

claim: Within the cluster of sarcoma genes evaluated, the top-scoring cellular functions were cell cycle control and cell division.
source: Indeed, within the cluster of sarcoma genes evaluated, the top-scoring cellular functions were cell cycle control and cell division (Hettmer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hettmer et al., 2011) describing the gene cluster.

claim: The list of candidate targets included genes encoding 3 other enzymes relevant for amino acid biosynthesis: branched chain aminotransferase 1 (BCAT1), phosphoserine aminotransferase (PSAT1) and phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH).
source: However, we note that in addition to ASNS, our list of candidate targets included genes encoding 3 other enzymes relevant for amino acid biosynthesis: branched chain aminotransferase 1 (BCAT1), phosphoserine aminotransferase (PSAT1) and phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH).
evidence: The claim is an explicit statement about the genes included in the screen.

claim: Both PHGDH and PSAT1 contribute to serine/glycine biosynthesis, which plays an important role in supporting nucleotide synthesis in rapidly proliferating cells.
source: Both PHGDH and PSAT1 contribute to serine/ glycine biosynthesis, which plays an important role in supporting nucleotide synthesis in rapidly proliferating cells (Jain et al., 2012; Labuschagne et al., 2014), and recent publications indicate that high expression of PHGDH in tumor tissue is required for cell growth in epithelial malignancies (Locasale et al., 2011; Possemato et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Jain et al., 2012; Labuschagne et al., 2014) on serine/glycine biosynthesis.

claim: High expression of PHGDH in tumor tissue is required for cell growth in epithelial malignancies.
source: Both PHGDH and PSAT1 contribute to serine/ glycine biosynthesis, which plays an important role in supporting nucleotide synthesis in rapidly proliferating cells (Jain et al., 2012; Labuschagne et al., 2014), and recent publications indicate that high expression of PHGDH in tumor tissue is required for cell growth in epithelial malignancies (Locasale et al., 2011; Possemato et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Locasale et al., 2011; Possemato et al., 2011) on PHGDH in epithelial cancers.

claim: Silencing of PSAT1, PHGDH or BCAT1 did not inhibit sarcoma cell growth.
source: However, in our screen, silencing of PSAT1, PHGDH or BCAT1 did not inhibit sarcoma cell growth (Supplementary files 5–6), suggesting that these biosynthetic pathways may be of lesser importance for the sarcomatous malignancies studied here.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the shRNA screen shown in Supplementary files 5-6.

claim: Serine/glycine biosynthetic pathways may be of lesser importance for the sarcomatous malignancies studied here.
source: However, in our screen, silencing of PSAT1, PHGDH or BCAT1 did not inhibit sarcoma cell growth (Supplementary files 5–6), suggesting that these biosynthetic pathways may be of lesser importance for the sarcomatous malignancies studied here.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the negative results for PSAT1, PHGDH, and BCAT1 in the screen.

claim: ASNS expression among tissues in adult animals varies considerably.
source: ASNS expression among tissues in adult animals varies considerably (Balasubramanian et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Balasubramanian et al., 2013) on ASNS expression patterns.

claim: ASNS in tumor tissue has been linked to the transactivating effects of oncogenic effectors such as TP53 and metabolic stress.
source: ASNS in tumor tissue has been linked to the transactivating effects of oncogenic effectors such as TP53 (Scian et al., 2004) and metabolic stress (Balasubramanian et al., 2013; Cui et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Scian et al., 2004; Balasubramanian et al., 2013; Cui et al., 2007) on ASNS regulation.

claim: In pancreatic cancer, glucose deprivation upregulated ASNS expression, which protected tumor cells from apoptosis induced by glucose deprivation.
source: For example, in pancreatic cancer, glucose deprivation upregulated ASNS expression, which, in turn, protected tumor cells from apoptosis induced by glucose deprivation itself (Cui et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Cui et al., 2007) on ASNS in pancreatic cancer.

claim: Upregulation of ASNS in response to amino acid restriction is part of a normal physiological adaptation response to counteract nutrient deprivation.
source: Similarly, upregulation of ASNS in response to amino acid restriction, such as plasma asparagine depletion by treatment with asparaginase (Cui et al., 2007), is part of a normal physiological adaptation response to counteract nutrient deprivation (Balasubramanian et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Cui et al., 2007; Balasubramanian et al., 2013) on ASNS regulation.

claim: As sarcomas outgrow the existing vasculature, tumor cells are continuously exposed to a microenvironment in which the supply of nutrients is limited.
source: As sarcomas outgrow the existing vasculature, tumor cells are continuously exposed to a microenvironment in which the supply of nutrients is limited.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about tumor biology and nutrient availability.

claim: Increased Asns mRNA expression in Kras;p16p19null mouse sarcomas compared to normal muscle could occur in response to amino acid and glucose deprivation in rapidly growing sarcomas.
source: Increased Asns mRNA expression in Kras;p16p19null mouse sarcomas as compared to normal muscle could occur in response to amino acid and glucose deprivation in rapidly growing sarcomas.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on known ASNS regulation and tumor microenvironment.

claim: Cellular asparagine reliance has been exploited successfully in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) with bacterially derived asparaginase.
source: Cellular asparagine reliance has been exploited successfully in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) with bacterially derived asparaginase (Haskell et al., 1969; Jaffe et al., 1971; Richards and Kilberg, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Haskell et al., 1969; Jaffe et al., 1971; Richards and Kilberg, 2006) on asparaginase in ALL treatment.

claim: Lymphoblasts are thought to be exquisitely sensitive to asparaginase treatment due to their low ASNS expression.
source: Lymphoblasts are thought to be exquisitely sensitive to asparaginase treatment due to their low ASNS expression (Richards and Kilberg, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Richards and Kilberg, 2006) on asparaginase sensitivity.

claim: Growth inhibitory effects of asparaginase on sarcoma cells in vitro were previously reported by Tardito et al.
source: Growth inhibitory effects of asparaginase on sarcoma cells in vitro were previously reported by Tardito et al (Tardito et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Tardito et al., 2006) on asparaginase effects on sarcoma cells.

claim: The response of sarcoma cells to asparaginase alone is moderate to poor when compared to the published spectrum of asparaginase sensitivity of primary lymphoblasts.
source: However, the response of sarcoma cells to asparaginase alone is moderate to poor (Figure 4A, (Tardito et al., 2006)) when compared to the published spectrum of asparaginase sensitivity of primary lymphoblasts (EC50 concentrations between <0.002 and >10 IU/ml; (Fine et al., 2005)).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data from Figure 4A with cited literature (Fine et al., 2005) on lymphoblast sensitivity.

claim: One published report on the efficacy of asparaginase as a single agent documented remissions in 7 of 32 children with ALL, but there was no objective response in a single patient with RMS.
source: One published report on the efficacy of asparaginase as a single agent documented remissions in 7 of 32 children with ALL, but there was no objective response in a single patient with RMS (Jaffe et al., 1971).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Jaffe et al., 1971) on asparaginase clinical efficacy.

claim: Asparaginase is a well-characterized drug with a relatively favorable toxicity profile that does not overlap with the toxicities of conventional cytostatics used in RMS treatment.
source: Yet, asparaginase is a well-characterized drug with a relatively favorable toxicity profile that does not overlap with the toxicities of conventional cytostatics used in RMS treatment (Haskell et al., 1969), and the further development of specific, cell-permeable chemical inhibitors of ASNS may open additional therapeutic opportunities (Richards and Kilberg, 2006), especially when combined with systemic asparagine depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Haskell et al., 1969) on asparaginase toxicity.

claim: The further development of specific, cell-permeable chemical inhibitors of ASNS may open additional therapeutic opportunities, especially when combined with systemic asparagine depletion.
source: Yet, asparaginase is a well-characterized drug with a relatively favorable toxicity profile that does not overlap with the toxicities of conventional cytostatics used in RMS treatment (Haskell et al., 1969), and the further development of specific, cell-permeable chemical inhibitors of ASNS may open additional therapeutic opportunities (Richards and Kilberg, 2006), especially when combined with systemic asparagine depletion.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about future therapeutic development based on the study findings.

claim: Understanding the molecular networks that support sarcoma cell proliferation may enable the development of therapies based on selective targeting of proliferation-relevant cellular pathways.
source: Understanding the molecular networks that support sarcoma cell proliferation may enable the development of therapies based on selective targeting of proliferation-relevant cellular pathways.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the potential impact of the research.

claim: This study identified asparagine starvation as a candidate intervention that impedes sarcoma growth.
source: This study identified asparagine starvation as a candidate intervention that impedes sarcoma growth.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: It is highly unlikely that any interventions will have noticeable anti-sarcoma effects in vivo when used alone.
source: Yet, it is highly unlikely that any interventions will have noticeable anti-sarcoma effects in vivo when used alone.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that ASNS silencing alone did not delay tumor growth.

claim: For future studies and clinical development, it will be important to rationally select combinations of interventions that target multiple proliferation-relevant cellular processes including asparagine reliance of sarcoma cells.
source: For future studies and clinical development, it will be important to rationally select combinations of interventions that target multiple proliferation-relevant cellular processes including Asparagine reliance of sarcoma cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about future research directions.

claim: Kras;p16p19null satellite cells typically gave rise to RMS, whereas the identical oncogenetic lesions introduced into fibroadipogenic precursors almost always produced sarcomas lacking myogenic differentiation features (non-myogenic sarcomas, NMS).
source: The myogenic differentiation status of the Ras-driven sarcomas generated in this system depends largely on the cell type transduced, also known as the "cell-of-origin": Kras; p16p19null satellite cells typically gave rise to RMS, whereas the identical oncogenetic lesions introduced into fibroadipogenic precursors within the MFA cell pool almost always produced sarcomas lacking myogenic differentiation features (non-myogenic sarcomas, NMS) (Hettmer et al., 2011)(Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hettmer et al., 2011) and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kras;p16p19null mouse sarcomas from each of these cellular origins recapitulate transcriptional profiles across the entire spectrum of human RMS.
source: We previously showed that Kras;p16p19null mouse sarcomas from each of these cellular origins recapitulate transcriptional profiles across the entire spectrum of human RMS and used this information to identify 141 genes of potential significance for sarcoma growth (Hettmer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hettmer et al., 2011) on transcriptional profiling.

claim: 141 genes of potential significance for sarcoma growth were identified from transcriptional profiling of Kras;p16p19null mouse sarcomas.
source: We previously showed that Kras;p16p19null mouse sarcomas from each of these cellular origins recapitulate transcriptional profiles across the entire spectrum of human RMS and used this information to identify 141 genes of potential significance for sarcoma growth (Hettmer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hettmer et al., 2011) describing the gene identification.

claim: A customized shRNA proliferation screen was designed using 5 distinct shRNAs per candidate gene.
source: To evaluate the functional contributions of each of the previously identified sarcoma-relevant genes, we designed a customized shRNA proliferation screen, using 5 distinct shRNAs per candidate gene (Supplementary files 1–4).
evidence: The claim is an explicit description of the experimental design.

claim: The screen was carried out in one Kras;p16p19null RMS and one Kras;p16p19null NMS cell line.
source: The screen was carried out in one Kras;p16p19null RMS and one Kras;p16p19null NMS cell line, and shRNAs were delivered in puromycin-selectable pLKO lentiviral vectors.
evidence: The claim is an explicit description of the experimental design.

claim: Correlation coefficients of 0.8348 and 0.9501 between puromycin-treated and untreated cells confirmed adequate transduction efficiencies.
source: Correlation coefficients of 0.8348 and 0.9501 between puromycin-treated and untreated cells confirmed adequate transduction efficiencies (Figure 1A,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 1A,F.

claim: ShRNA mediated silencing of Kras (G12v)-IRES-GFP markedly inhibits the growth of Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells.
source: As shRNA mediated silencing of Kras (G12v)-IRES-GFP, the driver oncogene used to initiate the mouse sarcomas, markedly inhibits the growth of Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B), shRNAs directed against either GFP or KRAS served as positive controls in this screen and showed clear growth-inhibitory effects (Figure 1C–D, 1H-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: ShRNAs directed against either GFP or KRAS served as positive controls in this screen and showed clear growth-inhibitory effects.
source: As shRNA mediated silencing of Kras (G12v)-IRES-GFP, the driver oncogene used to initiate the mouse sarcomas, markedly inhibits the growth of Kras;p16p19null sarcoma cells (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B), shRNAs directed against either GFP or KRAS served as positive controls in this screen and showed clear growth-inhibitory effects (Figure 1C–D, 1H-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D, 1H-I.

claim: Control shRNAs directed against LACZ, red fluorescent protein (RFP) and luciferase (LUC) served as negative controls and showed no growth-inhibitory effects.
source: Control shRNAs (cntrl-shRNA) directed against LACZ, red fluorescent protein (RFP) and luciferase (LUC) served as negative controls, and showed no growth-inhibitory effects (Figure 1C–D, 1H-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D, 1H-I.

claim: Receiver operator curve (ROC) analysis validated the ability of this system to distinguish between shRNAs with and without growth-inhibitory effects on sarcoma cell proliferation.
source: Receiver operator curve (ROC) analysis, using an external control set of shGFP-infected and cntrl-shRNA-infected RMS and NMS cells (Supplementary files 3–4), validated the ability of this system to distinguish between shRNAs with and without growth-inhibitory effects on sarcoma cell proliferation (Figure 1B,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis data shown in Figure 1B,G.

claim: ROC analysis determined a false discovery rate of <30% for shRNAs associated with a reduction in proliferation to <52% of the average of cntrl-shRNA-infected RMS cells.
source: ROC analysis also determined a false discovery rate of <30% for shRNAs associated with a reduction in proliferation to <52% of the average of cntrl-shRNA-infected RMS cells (Figure 1B–C) and <40% of cntrl-shRNA-infected NMS cells (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: ROC analysis determined a false discovery rate of <30% for shRNAs associated with a reduction in proliferation to <40% of cntrl-shRNA-infected NMS cells.
source: ROC analysis also determined a false discovery rate of <30% for shRNAs associated with a reduction in proliferation to <52% of the average of cntrl-shRNA-infected RMS cells (Figure 1B–C) and <40% of cntrl-shRNA-infected NMS cells (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Soft-tissue sarcomas (STS) are a heterogeneous group of non-hematopoietic, mesodermal cancers.
source: Soft-tissue sarcomas (STS) are a heterogeneous group of non-hematopoietic, mesodermal cancers.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sarcoma classification.

claim: Certain STS types present with tissue-specific features, such as skeletal muscle differentiation in rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS).
source: Certain STS types present with tissue-specific features, such as skeletal muscle differentiation in rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) (Parham and Barr, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Parham and Barr, 2013) on RMS characteristics.

claim: For most STS tumors, cure depends on radical resection and/or radiation of the tumor.
source: For most STS tumors, cure depends on radical resection and/or radiation of the tumor, and therapeutic options for tumors that have spread regionally and/or systemically are limited (Linch et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Linch et al., 2014) on STS treatment.

claim: Therapeutic options for tumors that have spread regionally and/or systemically are limited.
source: For most STS tumors, cure depends on radical resection and/or radiation of the tumor, and therapeutic options for tumors that have spread regionally and/or systemically are limited (Linch et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Linch et al., 2014) on STS treatment limitations.

claim: The genetic spectrum of STS is heterogeneous.
source: The genetic spectrum of STS is heterogeneous.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about STS genetics.

claim: Many STS tumors carry complex karyotypes with variable genetic changes; others express specific oncogenic mutations or exclusive chromosomal translocations within a relatively simple karyotype.
source: Many tumors carry complex karyotypes with variable genetic changes; others express specific oncogenic mutations or exclusive chromosomal translocations within a relatively simple karyotype (Bovee and Hogendoorn, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Bovee and Hogendoorn, 2010) on STS genetics.

claim: For RMS, two main genotypes have been described: those characterized by expression of the fusion oncogenes PAX3:FOXO1 or PAX7:FOXO1 and those that lack these fusions.
source: For RMS, two main genotypes have been described: those characterized by expression of the fusion oncogenes PAX3:FOXO1 or PAX7:FOXO1 and those that lack these fusions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about RMS classification.

claim: The most common oncogenic mutations in fusion-negative RMS tumors are in the Ras pathway.
source: The most common oncogenic mutations in the latter group of fusion-negative RMS tumors are in the Ras pathway (Shern et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Shern et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013) on RMS genetics.

claim: Small molecules targeting asparagine availability could be useful as anti-sarcoma therapeutics.
source: Thus, small molecules targeting asparagine availability (Richards and Kilberg, 2006) could be useful as anti-sarcoma therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the study findings and cited literature on ASNS inhibitors.

claim: Adequate availability of asparagine is required in rapidly proliferating sarcomas cells, likely to support nascent polypeptide synthesis.
source: We found that adequate availability of asparagine is required in rapidly proliferating sarcomas cells, likely to support nascent polypeptide synthesis, and that asparagine starvation impedes sarcoma growth.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the OP-puromycin and proliferation data showing that asparagine starvation impedes protein synthesis and cell growth.

claim: Asparagine starvation impedes sarcoma growth.
source: We found that adequate availability of asparagine is required in rapidly proliferating sarcomas cells, likely to support nascent polypeptide synthesis, and that asparagine starvation impedes sarcoma growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by the proliferation and in vivo data showing that asparagine depletion reduces sarcoma growth.
